newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.African white ex-rulers deny blame for massacre.
newsitem.headline: S.African white ex-rulers deny blame for massacre.

text.p: South Africa's former white rulers on Monday blamed a 1992 massacre in which 29 people died on the African National Congress and the leader of a black homeland.

The Truth and Reconciliation commission held its second hearing into the Bisho massacre in which 28 members of the ANC, now the ruling party, were killed during a protest march on the capital of the nominally independent black homeland of Ciskei.

The Ciskei Defence Force of Oupa Gqozo fired on marchers led by Ronnie Kasrils, a member of the South African Communist Party who is now deputy minister of defence. One of the Ciskei troops also died.
On Monday, the National Party -- which was in power at the time of the killing -- said the ANC and Gqozo were to blame.

"Those who were killed and wounded at Bisho were at the wrong place at the wrong time, being led by irresponsible and reckless leaders against a tyrant," said the National Party submission presented by former defence minister Roelf Meyer and former police minister Hernus Kriel.
"Although all measures had been taken to try and safeguard a peaceful outcome, they paid the ultimate price for reasons we may still not fully comprehend."
Ciskei and other homelands were disbanded after the April 1994 all-race elections in which the ANC swept the National Party from power.
The truth commission, headed by Nobel peace prize winner Desmond Tutu, is to compile as full a picture as possible of human rights abuses during 33 years of apartheid war.

In Pietermaritzburg, the commission heard allegations that police sided with the Inkatha Freedom Party during a week of battles between Inkatha members and ANC rivals in 1990 in which about 150 people were killed.
"We expected to be able to run to the police for safety but they just shot at us and killed us," said Thulani Mbanjwa, a survivor of the fighting near Pietermaritzburg in KwaZulu-Natal province.
The clashes were among the worst in the province, where more than 15,000 people are estimated to have died in a decade of political violence that erupted in the mid-1980s.
